conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is supporting new mothers just like you. In a moment we’ll go through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a quick, well-studied list of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Everything you say is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification anytime. Ready to start?

Thinking back over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has that been most of the time, sometimes, not very often, or almost never?

*sighs softly, then offers a small smile*

I guess... sometimes? I still laugh when my husband does something silly to try to cheer me up, or when the baby makes those funny faces while sleeping. But it's not like before - I used to laugh so easily, and now it feels like I have to remind myself to find things funny. Yesterday my friend sent me a hilarious meme and I just... couldn't really get into it. I smiled, but it felt forced.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, just not as easily as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shifts in the chair, eyes on the floor for a second*

Most days… not really. I mean, I used to get excited about little things—grabbing a fancy coffee, even just a quiet shower. Now when I think about tomorrow, all I see is the same cycle of feed, burp, change, try to sleep, repeat. I still look forward to my mom bringing dinner on Tuesdays, but the feeling’s kind of flat—like I know I’ll appreciate it, yet the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quietly* Yeah... I do that. Like when the baby wouldn't settle the other night, I kept thinking maybe I ate something that made my milk upset her stomach. Or if she cries for a long time, I wonder if I'm doing something wrong as a mom. It's not all the time, but sometimes I'll just be sitting there rocking her and these thoughts creep in that maybe I'm not doing enough, or that other moms seem to handle this better than me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods slowly, twisting a tissue in my hands*

Yes... it's like there's this constant low hum of worry in the back of my mind. Even when everything seems fine - the baby's sleeping, my husband's home - I'll suddenly feel my chest get tight thinking about whether she's breathing okay, or if that tiny rash is something serious. Last night I found myself googling about SIDS at 3 AM even though she's perfectly healthy. I know these thoughts aren't logical, but I can't seem to stop them from popping up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*presses a hand to chest*

Sometimes, yeah. It’s different from the everyday worry—this comes out of nowhere. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. It passes pretty quickly, usually if I step outside or splash cold water on my face, but for those minutes it feels like something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily*

Yeah... most days, honestly. It's like I'm drowning in little things - the laundry pile, the dishes, trying to find time to shower. Yesterday I just sat on the floor crying when the baby spilled milk on the couch because it felt like one more thing I couldn't handle. I used to be so organized before, and now even making a simple decision like what to eat feels overwhelming. My husband keeps telling me to ask for help, but I feel like I should be able to manage this, you know.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls cardigan tighter around shoulders*

It’s more that I can’t settle, even when the baby’s out cold. I lie there running through tomorrow’s feed times, wondering if her sniffle is getting worse, replaying every little thing I did “wrong.” Some nights I drop off fine, then jolt awake at 3 a.m. with my mind racing and can’t get back to sleep for an hour or more. I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy” I can’t sleep—it’s more this restless, keyed-up feeling that keeps me tossing.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes glisten, voice drops*

Yeah... it's like this heavy feeling that just sits on my chest some days. Not every day - like yesterday I felt okay when my sister visited. But then this morning I was feeding the baby and suddenly felt this wave of sadness for no reason. I looked at her perfect little face and instead of feeling happy, I just felt... empty. I cried in the shower so my husband wouldn't see. It's not all the time, but it's there enough that I notice it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shrugs one shoulder, voice small*

Not really. I got teary in the shower this morning, but actual crying—like, really letting go—hasn’t happened since last week. I feel low and my eyes might sting, yet I manage to choke it back most of the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No, never. I would never do that to my baby or my family. Even on my worst days, that thought has never crossed my mind.

I hear how hard you're working to care for your baby while feeling like the joy and spark have drained away. You described a constant hum of worry, sudden panicky moments, and a heavy sadness that catches you off-guard-even when you're looking at your beautiful baby. At the same time, you're still able to laugh sometimes and you clearly love your family, which makes the weight you're carrying feel all the more confusing.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports pervasive loss of anticipatory joy, describing even previously pleasant events as "flat" and lacking "spark," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, specific self-blame episodes that occur "some of the time," directly matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, irrational worries occurring "very often" despite recognizing they lack logic, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected panic episodes that come out of nowhere and resolve quickly, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent middle-of-the-night insomnia driven by anxious rumination, matching "Yes, sometimes" even though she avoids the word "unhappy."</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences noticeable, recurrent sadness that disrupts bonding and daily life, matching "Yes, quite often".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you at 19/30, well above the 14-point threshold that flags probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. You endorsed loss of interest/enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), daily guilt (<quote>other moms handle this better</quote>), pervasive worry and panic symptoms, impaired coping (<quote>drowning in little things</quote>), and early-morning insomnia driven by rumination. These map onto five core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest, guilt/worthlessness, diminished ability to think/concentrate (decisional paralysis), and sleep disturbance. You denied self-harm thoughts, so immediate safety risk is low, but severity warrants urgent follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer-support groups, or <med>sertraline</med>/other compatible medications if recommended
3. Share these results with your partner or a trusted family member so they can help coordinate care and overnight rest
4. Begin gentle daily structure: 20 min outdoor walk, balanced meals, and one 3-4 h block of uninterrupted night sleep (partner gives a bottle or does the first resettle)
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Keep crisis numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local 24-h postpartum support warmline
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Self-report on EPDS-10 items (responses recorded verbatim):

<sym>Symptom clusters endorsed:</sym>
- Anhedonia: diminished ability to laugh/look forward to events; describes pleasure as “flat”
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“maybe I ate something… other moms handle this better”)
- Persistent, intrusive worry (“low hum of worry,” 3 a.m. SIDS searching) with episodic panic symptoms (sudden racing heart, breathlessness)
- Overwhelm / impaired coping (“drowning in little things,” decisional difficulty, tearfulness over minor mishaps)
- Mood-congruent sleep disturbance (can’t “settle,” early-morning rumination)
- Sad / empty mood with near-daily tearfulness (choked back), not pervasive but noticeable to patient
- Denies any self-harm ideation

<med>Screening significance:</med>
Meets ≥5 mood/anxiety items at clinical threshold; pattern most consistent with postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety symptoms. No safety concerns (zero self-harm endorsement). Patient aware of change from baseline functioning.

<risk>Risk factors documented:</risk>
- Anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness, sleep disruption, feeling overwhelmed
- Absence of suicidal ideation (protective factor)

<plan>Next steps discussed:</plan>
- Reviewed results; recommended formal evaluation for diagnosis and treatment planning
- Provided crisis resources; safety plan reviewed
